claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% boron to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability relative to the undoped alloy.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% boron will improve the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state relative to the undoped alloy.
The proposed intervention is the addition of about 1–2 at.% boron during alloy synthesis.
The beneficial effect should occur under rapid-solidification conditions where the cooling rate is near the critical threshold for glass formation.
The beneficial effect should be limited to a narrow boron-concentration range.
Boron addition will enhance atomic-packing disorder.
Boron addition will increase topological frustration.
Enhanced packing disorder and topological frustration will retard nucleation of crystalline phases.
Boron atoms have a small atomic size and high chemical-bonding affinity in the proposed alloy context.
Boron will disturb the alloy's local short-range and medium-range order.
Disruption of local order will increase the energy barrier for crystallization.
The increased crystallization barrier will reduce the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
The increased crystallization barrier will elevate the crystallization-onset temperature measured by DSC.
Boron-doped samples will have a lower critical cooling rate for amorphization than otherwise identical boron-free samples.
Boron-doped samples will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than otherwise identical boron-free samples.
Boron concentrations above the proposed low-concentration range may promote boride-phase formation.
Boride formation or embrittlement at excessive boron concentrations would negate the proposed glass-forming benefit.
The magnitude of the changes in critical cooling rate and crystallization temperature may depend on overall alloy composition and processing parameters.
